title: NABH Standards & Patient Safety
shortDescription: How NABH's ten chapters translate into everyday hospital workflows — identification, medication safety, infection control, consent, and how an incident actually gets handled.
genZNote: Patient safety isn't a chapter you read once. It's a workflow that runs every single shift.

sections.heading: Core Patient-Safety Elements
bullets: Patient identification — using at least two identifiers before any procedure, medication, or sample collection, to prevent wrong-patient errors.
Medication safety — controls at prescribing, dispensing, and administration to prevent errors, especially with look-alike/sound-alike drugs and high-risk medications.
Infection prevention and control — hand hygiene, sterilisation, surveillance, and (current focus) antimicrobial stewardship.
Informed consent and patient rights — patients understand and agree to procedures, and know their rights within the care process.
Communication and clinical documentation — accurate handover and record-keeping, since most safety failures involve a communication gap somewhere.
Emergency care readiness — defined processes and trained staff for time-critical situations.

sections.heading: From Incident to Improvement
sections.body: When something goes wrong — or nearly goes wrong — hospitals don't just document it and move on. There's a defined workflow connecting the event to a system-level fix.

steps.name: Incident occurs or is identified
steps.explanation: An adverse event, near-miss, or sentinel event (a serious, often preventable event causing significant harm) happens or is caught.
steps.purpose: The trigger for the entire safety-improvement cycle.

steps.name: Incident reporting
steps.explanation: The event is documented through the hospital's incident-reporting system, often with a no-blame culture to encourage honest reporting.
steps.purpose: You can't fix what isn't reported.

steps.name: Investigation and risk management
steps.explanation: Root cause analysis (RCA) identifies the underlying system failure, not just the individual action.
steps.purpose: Prevents 'blame the person' fixes that don't actually stop recurrence.

steps.name: Corrective action and monitoring
steps.explanation: A system-level fix is implemented and its effectiveness is tracked through quality indicators over time.
steps.purpose: Closes the loop — the same corrective-action pattern used across this entire subject.

sections.heading: Quality Indicators and Patient Experience
sections.body: NABH tracks both objective quality indicators (infection rates, medication error rates) and subjective patient experience (satisfaction, communication quality) — they are related but distinct, and both matter for accreditation.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: NABH's patient-safety standards translate into concrete hospital workflows — identification, medication safety, infection control, consent, and a defined incident-to-corrective-action cycle.
keyFacts: Patient identification requires at least two identifiers before high-risk actions.
A sentinel event is a serious, often preventable event causing significant patient harm.
Root cause analysis targets the SYSTEM failure, not just the individual who made the error.
Patient safety (objective harm prevention) and patient experience/satisfaction (subjective perception) are related but distinct measures.
commonConfusion: Patient safety and patient satisfaction are often assumed to move together, but a patient can report high satisfaction despite an undetected safety lapse, or low satisfaction despite technically safe care — they are measured and managed separately.

highYieldFacts: Two-identifier patient identification is a foundational, cross-cutting safety requirement.
RCA targets systems, not individuals — this is central to a genuine no-blame safety culture.
Sentinel events specifically denote serious, often preventable harm — not every incident is a sentinel event.
commonTraps: Assuming an incident-reporting culture exists to assign blame — it's designed to surface system gaps.
mustRemember: Incident → Report → Investigate (RCA) → Corrective action → Monitor — the same closed loop, applied to patient safety.

confusedTerms.distinction: Patient safety measures objective freedom from preventable harm; patient satisfaction measures the patient's subjective experience of care. A hospital can score well on one and poorly on the other.

possibleQuestions: Describe the workflow from a reported incident to a system-level corrective action in a hospital setting.

sources.name: NABH — National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare Providers

comparisons.distinction: Patient safety is about objectively preventing harm; patient satisfaction is about the patient's subjective experience of care. Both are tracked, but they are not the same measure.

questions.prompt: Root cause analysis (RCA) after an incident is primarily aimed at:
options: Identifying which staff member to discipline
Identifying the underlying system failure that allowed the incident
Closing the incident report as quickly as possible
questions.explanation: RCA targets systemic causes, not individual blame — central to an effective patient-safety culture.

questions.prompt: True or False: High patient satisfaction scores guarantee that patient safety standards are being met.
questions.explanation: Satisfaction and safety are related but distinct — a patient can be satisfied without an underlying safety lapse being detected.
